objects.doc: read, write, and edit workspace files
run shell commands in the workspace
the epic/issue board — decompose work into dispatchable issues
durable memories that survive context compaction
show yourself a file, a value, or a function's documentation — the only way material enters your context
fetch a program you already ran, and hand a patched copy back to be run
return your verdict on the work you are reviewing

meta.name: list
meta.doc: List the functions available on this API object, each as `{ name, summary }`. Only the functions this run actually bound are returned, so the directory never names a call your program cannot make. Open a view of one function's full signature, argument descriptions and types with `view.openDocsView`.

session.name: finish

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What you did, in a sentence or two.

session.doc: End your session, reporting what you did in a sentence or two. This is the only thing that ends it. It does not stop your program — whatever follows it still runs — so call it last, once the tools have confirmed the work is really done. If your program then fails, the ending is cancelled and you get another turn.

session.name: approve
session.doc: Accept the work you are reviewing: it meets every completion criterion and stays in scope. This ends your session. It does not stop your program — whatever follows it still runs — so call it last, once you have actually read the change.

session.name: requestChanges

parameters.name: items
parameters.doc: Every change that must be made before the work can be accepted, one per entry: what is wrong, and what to change. It may not be empty.

session.doc: Reject the work you are reviewing, listing every change that must be made before it can be accepted. Each item says what is wrong and what to change; the list may not be empty. This ends your session, and does not stop your program.

views.name: openFile

signatures.signature: openFile(path: string, options?: { offset?: number; limit?: number; }): FileRead

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to open. Relative to your workspace, or absolute.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The window of lines to show; omit it to show the whole file.

fields.name: offset
fields.doc: The 1-based line to start at.

fields.name: limit
fields.doc: How many lines to show from `offset`.

views.doc: Read a file AND show it to yourself: you get back exactly what `fs.readFile` returns, and the file also becomes its own item in your context window, attributed to its path and closable by it. The split from `fs.readFile` is the point — `fs.readFile` gets bytes for your PROGRAM, `view.openFile` shows a file to YOU — so a program that reads forty files to grep them still puts nothing in your window. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the SAME page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image file is shown to you as a picture, and is the ONLY way to look at one — `fs.readFile` of an image describes it without showing it. Pictures are the one thing this call can refuse. Only so many image-carrying views may be open at once (your agent's `imageViewCap`); opening one past that throws `limit-exceeded` naming the cap, and nothing is opened and nothing is shown, so close one with `view.close(path)` and try again. Re-opening a picture you already have open replaces it rather than adding one, and is never refused. Text views are never refused by this cap.

views.name: openText

parameters.name: label
parameters.doc: What to file the view under. It is what `view.close` takes, and opening the same label again replaces what it showed. It may not be empty.

parameters.name: body
parameters.doc: What to show yourself. An empty body is allowed: it is how you say that something you were showing is now empty.

views.doc: Show yourself a value your program computed, under `label` — a directory listing, a command's output, a child agent's answer, a table you assembled. This is what replaced `console.log` as the channel into your context: logs go to the run's operator, views come back to you on your next turn. Opening the same `label` again replaces what it showed, so a program may refine a view in a loop without piling up a copy per iteration. An empty label is `invalid-argument` — a view with no selector could never be closed or attributed — while an empty BODY is allowed, since it is how you say that something you were showing is now empty. A body or label over gg's caps throws `limit-exceeded` naming the cap; nothing is ever silently truncated.

views.name: openDocsView

parameters.name: target
parameters.doc: The function to document — the function itself (`fs.readFile`) or its name (`"readFile"`).

views.doc: Show yourself the full documentation for one function: its signature, its description, and the declarations of any types it refers to that you have not already been shown this session. Pass the function itself (`view.openDocsView(fs.readFile)`) or its name (`view.openDocsView("readFile")`). This is how you read what a function does. It is a **view**, not a return value — the documentation arrives in your next prompt under a `Documentation` heading keyed by the function name, exactly as a file or a computed value arrives — so it is not available in the turn you ask for it. Plan for that: ask in one turn, use it in the next. Opening the same function's docs again replaces the view rather than adding a second copy, and `view.close(name)` closes it when you are done with it. An unknown or unbound name throws `not-found`; `<object>.list()` is how you find out which names exist.

views.name: close

parameters.name: selector
parameters.doc: What the view is filed under: a file's path, a text view's label, or a documentation view's function name.

views.doc: Close every view carrying `selector` — for a file that is every page of that path, for a text view the one with that label, for a documentation view the function's name — and return how many were closed, freeing the tokens they occupied. Closing a selector that is not open returns `0` rather than failing, so a program that tidies up unconditionally does not have to guard every call. Closing a file view forgets what you read, not what exists; closing a text view discards the only copy of what it held, so write anything you will need later to a file or a memory first.

views.name: current
views.doc: List what is open in your context window right now: each view's `kind`, the `selector` that closes it, roughly what it costs you in `tokens`, and — for a paged file view — the `region` it covers. It is called `current` rather than `list` because every API object already carries a `list()` that lists that object's own functions. Read it before deciding what to close when your window is filling up.

programs.name: history
programs.doc: The programs you have already run this session, oldest first — each with the turn it ran on, how big it was, and whether it ran to its end. It lists shapes, not sources: fetch the one you want with `programs.get(turn)`. The list survives a compaction, so it is also how you find a program whose text has left your context window. An agent with no program library throws `unavailable`. It is empty — never an error — for one that has a library and has run nothing yet.

programs.name: get

parameters.name: turn
parameters.doc: The turn whose program to fetch, as `programs.history()` reports it. Omit it for your most recent one.

programs.doc: The exact source of one program you ran, as a string. With no argument, your most recent one. This is the first half of fixing a program without rewriting it: get what ran, patch it with ordinary string work (`replace`, `replaceAll`, a template literal), and hand the result to `programs.rerun`. What comes back is the program that **executed** — so when a turn's program was itself handed over by `programs.rerun`, you get the program that ran, not the few lines that asked for it, and fetch-patch-run composes turn after turn. A turn that ran no program, or one old enough that the library has dropped it, throws `not-found` naming the turns that are held; `programs.history()` lists them.

programs.name: rerun

parameters.name: source
parameters.doc: The program to run in place of this one. It may not be blank.

programs.doc: Hand gg a program to run in place of this one. Your program finishes, then gg compiles and runs `source` as this turn's program. Use it with `programs.get` to fix a program without re-emitting it. Nothing is undone: every call your program already made stands, and the program that runs next sees the world your program left behind — so hand over BEFORE doing work you do not want done twice. The first call stands; a second throws `refused`, because a silently replaced program is a change you cannot see. A blank source is `invalid-argument`. If your program then throws, the hand-over is cancelled along with everything else the failed program decided, and you get an ordinary error turn instead. Chains are bounded: hand over once per turn, and write the fixed program to do the work.

tools.name: shell

signatures.signature: shell(command: string, options?: { timeoutSecs?: number; }): ShellOutput

parameters.name: command
parameters.doc: The command line, run by `sh -c` with your workspace as its working directory.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: How to run it.

fields.name: timeoutSecs
fields.doc: How long to let it run before killing it. Defaults to 120, and is clamped to whatever is left of the run's wall-clock budget.

tools.doc: Run a command with `sh -c` in the workspace directory and return its merged stdout and stderr. A non-zero exit is NOT a failure — check `exitCode` on the result; only a process that could not be launched, or one the timeout killed, throws. `timeoutSecs` defaults to 120 and is clamped to whatever is left of the run's wall-clock budget. This run may **offload** shell output — the `shell` tool's own description says which mode is in force. Under `offload`, `output` holds only the tail that fits and ends with a note naming the two files the command's full stdout and stderr were written to. Under `adaptive` (the default), a command that **succeeded** returns no output at all, only that note; one that **failed** returns the tail. Grep the named files instead of re-running the command.

tools.name: readFile

signatures.signature: readFile(path: string, options?: { offset?: number; limit?: number; }): FileRead

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to read. Relative to your workspace, or absolute for anything else in this container.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The window of lines to read; omit it to read the whole file.

fields.name: offset
fields.doc: The 1-based line to start at. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

fields.name: limit
fields.doc: How many lines to return from `offset`. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

tools.doc: Read a file, returning either `{ kind: "text", ... }` or `{ kind: "image", ... }` — the format is detected from the file's bytes, never its extension. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines and are honoured only under a capped read policy. This gets bytes for your program and puts NOTHING in your context window; `view.openFile` is the call that shows the file to you. A relative path resolves against your workspace; an absolute one is read as given, so anything in this container — an offloaded command's output under `/tmp/gg-shell`, say — is readable. Throws `not-found` for a missing path. Reading an IMAGE describes it to your program — label, media type, byte size — and does not show it to YOU: the pixels reach neither your program nor your context window, so a file you only `readFile` is a file you have not looked at. `view.openFile` is the one way to actually see a picture.

tools.name: writeFile

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: Where to write. Relative to your workspace, or absolute. Parent directories are created for you.

parameters.name: contents
parameters.doc: The UTF-8 text to write. It replaces the file entirely.

tools.doc: Write UTF-8 text to a file, creating parent directories and replacing any existing file, and return the number of bytes written. Writing is the expensive direction of the sandbox — rewriting more than a few dozen large files in one program exhausts its fuel budget, so split a large rewrite across several turns.

tools.name: editFile

signatures.signature: editFile(path: string, oldString: string, newString: string): void

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to edit.

parameters.name: oldString
parameters.doc: The exact text to find, including its whitespace. It must appear exactly once.

parameters.name: newString
parameters.doc: The text to put in its place. An empty string deletes the match.

tools.doc: Replace the one exact occurrence of `oldString` in a file with `newString`. Throws `not-found` when the text does not appear and `conflict` — with the number of matches — when it appears more than once; widen the surrounding context until the match is unique.

tools.name: listDir

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The directory to list; omit it for your workspace root.

tools.doc: List a directory, sorted by name; defaults to your workspace. Each entry carries a bare `name` — join it with the directory you listed — and its `kind`. An empty directory is an empty array, not a failure.

tools.name: readSkill

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The skill's name, as the system prompt lists it.

tools.doc: Read a skill by name and return its body with the front matter stripped; reading it also pins that body permanently into your context, so a skill you have read stays read. A skill may be **code** rather than prose, or as well as it. If it carries code, reading it binds that code at `lib.<key>` for the rest of your session and the reply names the key and what it exports. If it carries an on-use script, gg runs it once your program has ended, and whatever it shows you arrives on your next turn. Throws `not-found` — listing the skills that do exist — when the name is unknown.

tools.name: writeMemory

parameters.name: memory
parameters.doc: The memory to record. Its name must not already be taken.

tools.doc: Record a durable memory that survives context compaction, and return how much of the memory budget is now used. Throws `conflict` on a duplicate name and `limit-exceeded` when the body would breach the run's caps — revise or delete a memory rather than accruing more. A memory may also carry **code**. `code` is a TypeScript module whose exports are bound at `lib.<name>` in every later program you write, so a helper you get right once you never write again; `onUse` is a script gg runs the first time the memory comes into use, whose views reach you on your next turn. Neither is context — they cost you no window, are never shown back to you, and count against no body limit — and both are bounded on their own.

tools.name: updateMemory

parameters.name: memory
parameters.doc: The replacement, keyed on its `name`. Every other field replaces what the existing memory held, and an omitted one clears it.

tools.doc: Replace an existing memory's description and body, keyed on its `name`, and return the memory budget. Its `code` and `onUse` are replaced too — omitting them clears them. Throws `not-found` when no memory has that name.

tools.name: createMemory

parameters.name: memory
parameters.doc: The memory to record. Its `body` stays out of your context window until you read it, and its name must not already be taken.

tools.doc: Record a new memory whose contents are kept OUT of your context window until you read them, and return the memory budget. Give it a slug (letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.`), a one-line description — required where the run keeps an index, since that is the memory's line in it — and the initial contents. It may also carry `code` (a module bound at `lib.<name>` once you read the memory) and `onUse` (a script run on that first read). Throws `conflict` on a duplicate slug and `limit-exceeded` when the contents, or the index entry, would breach a limit.

tools.name: readMemory

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

tools.doc: Read one memory's full contents, by slug — the only thing that brings them into your context. If the memory carries code, reading it also loads that code: the reply names the `lib.<key>` it is bound at, and it stays bound for the rest of your session. Throws `not-found` when no memory has that slug.

tools.name: editMemory

signatures.signature: editMemory(edit: { name: string; search: string; replace: string; }): MemoryUsage

parameters.name: edit
parameters.type: { name: string; search: string; replace: string; }
parameters.doc: The revision to make.

fields.name: name
fields.doc: The slug of the memory to revise.

fields.name: search
fields.doc: The exact text to find in its contents. It must appear exactly once.

fields.name: replace
fields.doc: The text to put in its place.

tools.doc: Revise a memory in place by replacing the one exact occurrence of `search` with `replace`, and return the memory budget. Append by quoting the last line and replacing it with itself plus what you are adding. Throws `not-found` when the text does not appear, `conflict` when it appears more than once, `limit-exceeded` when the result would be too long, and `invalid-argument` when the edit would leave the memory empty — delete it instead.

tools.name: searchMemories

parameters.name: keywords
parameters.doc: The words to look for. Several specific words rank better than one sentence, because a memory is ranked by how many of them it mentions.

tools.doc: Find the memories mentioning any of `keywords`, best first: plain case-insensitive substring matching over each memory's slug, description and contents, ranked by how many of your keywords a memory mentions and then by how often. Pass several specific words rather than one sentence, then `readMemory` the hits worth having in full. Throws `invalid-argument` when every keyword is empty; a search that matches nothing is an empty array.

tools.name: deleteMemory

parameters.name: name
parameters.doc: The memory's slug.

tools.doc: Evict a memory by name, freeing room in the budget, and return what is left in use. Throws `not-found` when no memory has that name.

tools.name: addTask

signatures.signature: addTask(task: { id: string; title: string; description?: string; blockedBy?: string[]; }): TaskUsage

parameters.name: task
parameters.type: { id: string; title: string; description?: string; blockedBy?: string[]; }
parameters.doc: The task to add.

fields.name: id
fields.doc: The id you choose for it. It is what every other task call takes, and no two tasks may share one.

fields.name: title
fields.doc: A short line naming the work.

fields.name: description
fields.doc: What the work is, at whatever length is useful.

fields.name: blockedBy
fields.doc: The ids of the tasks that must be done before this one. Defaults to none.

tools.doc: Add a task to the task DAG and return the task budget. `blockedBy` names the tasks that must finish before this one and defaults to none. Throws `conflict` on a duplicate id or on an edge that would close a cycle.

tools.name: updateTask

signatures.signature: updateTask(id: string, patch: { title?: string; description?: string | null; status?: TaskStatus; }): void

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to revise.

parameters.name: patch
parameters.type: { title?: string; description?: string | null; status?: TaskStatus; }
parameters.doc: The fields to change. Supply at least one; an omitted field is left alone.

fields.name: title
fields.doc: The title to replace the old one with.

fields.name: description
fields.doc: The description to replace the old one with, or `null` to clear it.

fields.name: status
fields.doc: Where the task now stands.

tools.doc: Revise a task's title, description and/or status; supply at least one. An omitted `description` leaves it alone, `null` clears it, and a string replaces it. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: setBlockedBy

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task whose blockers to replace.

parameters.name: blockedBy
parameters.doc: The ids of every task that must now be done before it. An empty array clears them all.

tools.doc: Replace a task's whole blocker set; an empty array clears every blocker. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id and `conflict` when an edge would close a cycle.

tools.name: completeTask

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to mark done.

tools.doc: Mark a task done. Tasks it was blocking become actionable once every one of their blockers is done. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: removeTask

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The task to remove.

tools.doc: Remove a task and every blocker edge pointing at it, and return the task budget. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: createEpic

signatures.signature: createEpic(epic: { prefix: string; title: string; description: string; }): EpicCreated

parameters.name: epic
parameters.type: { prefix: string; title: string; description: string; }
parameters.doc: The epic to create.

fields.name: prefix
fields.doc: 3-6 letters naming it. Upper-cased, it becomes the epic's id and the stem its issues are numbered from.

fields.name: title
fields.doc: A short line naming the body of work.

fields.name: description
fields.doc: What the epic covers, for a reader who has not seen its issues.

tools.doc: Create an epic to group related issues. `prefix` is 3-6 letters naming the epic; it is upper-cased and becomes the epic's id, which is also what its issues are numbered from — a prefix of `auth` gives issues `AUTH-1`, `AUTH-2`, and so on. Returns that id and the board budget. Throws `invalid-argument` when the prefix is not 3-6 letters, and `conflict` when another epic already holds it.

tools.name: createIssue

signatures.signature: createIssue(issue: { title: string; description?: string; inScope: string; outOfScope: string; completionCriteria: string; blockedBy?: string[]; epicId?: string; agent: string; reviewers?: string[]; }): IssueCreated

parameters.name: issue
parameters.type: { title: string; description?: string; inScope: string; outOfScope: string; completionCriteria: string; blockedBy?: string[]; epicId?: string; agent: string; reviewers?: string[]; }
parameters.doc: The issue to create.

fields.name: title
fields.doc: A short line naming the work.

fields.name: description
fields.doc: What the work is. Written for a child agent with no other context.

fields.name: inScope
fields.doc: What the issue covers, precisely. Part of the brief a child agent is given.

fields.name: outOfScope
fields.doc: What the issue deliberately does not cover, so the work stops where you meant it to.

fields.name: completionCriteria
fields.doc: What must be true for the issue to be done. It is what a reviewer checks the work against.

fields.name: blockedBy
fields.doc: The ids of every issue that must be done before this one. Defaults to none.

fields.name: epicId
fields.doc: The id of an existing epic to group it under. Omit it to leave it ungrouped and numbered under `ISSUE`.

fields.name: agent
fields.doc: The agent the issue is dispatched to. It must be one you may spawn.

fields.name: reviewers
fields.doc: The agents that must approve the work, from that same set. Required when this run's reviewers feature is on.

tools.doc: Create a self-contained, dispatchable issue. Returns the id the board **assigned** it — numbered under its epic's prefix (`AUTH-1`, `AUTH-2`, …), or under `ISSUE` when it has no epic — together with the board budget; you do not choose the id, so keep the returned one to block a later issue on this one or to wait for it. `inScope`, `outOfScope` and `completionCriteria` are what a child agent is briefed from, so write them for a reader with no other context. `agent` names the agent the issue is dispatched to and must be one you may spawn; `reviewers` names the agents that must approve the work, from that same set, and is required when this run's reviewers feature is on. `blockedBy` defaults to none; `epicId` groups the issue under an existing epic. Throws `invalid-argument` when `agent` or a reviewer is not yours to assign, and `conflict` on a blocker edge that would close a cycle.

tools.name: updateIssue

signatures.signature: updateIssue(id: string, patch: { title?: string; description?: string | null; inScope?: string; outOfScope?: string; completionCriteria?: string; status?: IssueStatus; epicId?: string | null; }): void

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to revise.

parameters.name: patch
parameters.type: { title?: string; description?: string | null; inScope?: string; outOfScope?: string; completionCriteria?: string; status?: IssueStatus; epicId?: string | null; }
parameters.doc: The fields to change. Supply at least one; an omitted field is left alone.

fields.name: title
fields.doc: The title to replace the old one with.

fields.name: description
fields.doc: The description to replace the old one with, or `null` to clear it.

fields.name: inScope
fields.doc: The scope statement to replace the old one with.

fields.name: outOfScope
fields.doc: The non-scope statement to replace the old one with.

fields.name: completionCriteria
fields.doc: The completion criteria to replace the old ones with.

fields.name: status
fields.doc: Where the issue now stands.

fields.name: epicId
fields.doc: The epic to regroup it under, or `null` to detach it from the one it has.

tools.doc: Revise an issue; supply at least one field. An omitted field is left alone, `description: null` clears the description, and `epicId: null` detaches the issue from its epic. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: setIssueBlockedBy

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue whose blockers to replace.

parameters.name: blockedBy
parameters.doc: The ids of every issue that must now be done before it. An empty array clears them all.

tools.doc: Replace an issue's whole blocker set; an empty array clears every blocker. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id and `conflict` when an edge would close a cycle.

tools.name: removeEpic

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The epic to remove.

tools.doc: Remove an epic, keeping its issues and ungrouping them, and return the board budget. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: removeIssue

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to remove.

tools.doc: Remove an issue and every blocker edge pointing at it, and return the board budget. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: waitForIssue

parameters.name: id
parameters.doc: The issue to wait on. It may not be the issue you were assigned.

tools.doc: Register a wait on an issue and return an acknowledgement. It does not block inside your program — it records the wait and returns at once, so the rest of your program still runs; the suspension happens after the program ends, between turns. Once the program finishes the run suspends, freeing this agent's slot for others, until the issue is terminal (done, or failed if its assigned agent could not complete it), then resumes on the next turn. Use it to sequence your next turn's work behind an issue you depend on. You cannot wait on the issue you were assigned to implement. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: evictFileView

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file whose views to drop. Omit it to drop every file view you hold.

tools.doc: Drop the contents of files you have read out of your context window, freeing the tokens they occupy, and report what that reclaimed; omit `path` to drop every file view. The files on disk are untouched — this forgets what you read, not what exists.

tools.name: archiveThread

parameters.name: ranges
parameters.doc: The inclusive spans of turn numbers to move out of your window.

tools.doc: Move whole turns out of your context window and report what that reclaimed. Every result you are given carries a header with its turn number and roughly what holding it costs, so name the turns worth dropping: `ranges` is a list of inclusive spans, and `archiveThread([{ from: 4, to: 19 }])` archives turns 4 through 19. Your own messages in an archived turn are dropped; the results are kept and stay searchable with `searchArchive`.

tools.name: searchArchive

parameters.name: query
parameters.doc: The substring to look for. Matching is case-insensitive.

tools.doc: Search archived history for a case-insensitive substring, most recent first, up to 8 hits. Check `archiveEmpty` before reading `hits`: it distinguishes "nothing has been archived yet" from "the search ran and matched nothing", so you do not archive again believing the first archive failed.

tools.name: compact

parameters.name: summary
parameters.doc: What your restarted window opens with. Write it for your future self: everything not in it and not re-read from `files` is gone.

parameters.name: files
parameters.doc: The paths to read afresh into the restarted window. Defaults to none.

tools.doc: Compact your context window: the detailed thread is dropped and restarted from `summary`, plus a fresh read of each path in `files`. Your skills, memories and task list are kept as they are. You are asked to call this when your window is full, and every other call is refused until you do. It does NOT stop your program: it registers the request and returns, and the rewrite happens once your program has ended. Everything not in your summary and not in `files` is gone, so write the summary for your future self and name the files you will actually need in hand.

tools.name: spawnSubagent

signatures.signature: spawnSubagent(request: { agent: string; } & ({ prompt: string; } | { issueId: string; })): SubagentHandle

parameters.name: request
parameters.type: { agent: string; } & ({ prompt: string; } | { issueId: string; })
parameters.doc: The agent to run and the brief to run it on.

fields.name: agent
fields.doc: The agent profile to run the child as, from the ones you may spawn. It selects the child's model, tools and instructions.

fields.name: prompt
fields.doc: Self-contained instructions for the child. Give this or `issueId`, never both and never neither.

fields.name: issueId
fields.doc: The board issue to brief the child from. Give this or `prompt`, never both and never neither.

tools.doc: Delegate scoped work to a child agent and return its handle immediately — the child runs in parallel while your program continues. Name the `agent` to run it as (one of the agents you may spawn — the system prompt lists them; it selects the child's model, tools, and instructions) and brief it with exactly one of `prompt` (self-contained instructions) or `issueId` (a board issue). The child shares your workspace. Throws `limit-exceeded` at the delegation depth cap, and `invalid-argument` if `agent` is not one you may spawn.

tools.name: waitForSubagents

parameters.name: ids
parameters.doc: The children to wait for. Omit it to wait for every one still outstanding.

tools.doc: Block until the named children have finished — or, with no argument, until every outstanding child has — and collect their results in dispatch order. The run's wall-clock budget keeps running while you wait, so wait once for many children rather than once per child. Throws `not-found` for an unknown id.

tools.name: sendMessage

parameters.name: agentId
parameters.doc: The child to deliver to, as `spawnSubagent` returned it.

parameters.name: message
parameters.doc: What to put in its inbox. It reads it at its next turn.

tools.doc: Deliver a message to a running child agent's inbox; it reads the message at its next turn. Throws `not-found` for an unknown agent id and `conflict` when that child has already returned.

tools.name: transitionState

parameters.name: state
parameters.doc: The state to move on to, named the way you name an agent to spawn.

parameters.name: note
parameters.doc: The opening message the next state's agent sees.

tools.doc: Move the process you are running inside on to another of its states, naming the state the way you name an agent to spawn; `note` is the opening message the next state's agent sees. Bound only when a state machine is driving you and the state you are in has somewhere to go. Like `compact` it is registered rather than performed: the call validates the target, returns, and your program runs on to its end — the transition happens after that, because replacing your agent (and your window) mid-program would pull every remaining call out from under it. The FIRST declaration stands, and a second throws `refused`. Throws `invalid-argument` for a state you may not move to.

tools.name: exec

parameters.name: agent
parameters.doc: The agent to become, from the ones you may become.

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: Its opening message. It already has your whole conversation, so this is the instruction rather than a briefing.

tools.doc: Continue this session as a different agent: the named agent takes over from your next turn with its own model, tools and instructions, keeping every capability the two of you both have — your whole conversation above all, so it needs no catching up. `prompt` is its opening message. Registered rather than performed, exactly as `transitionState` is and for the same reason: your window would otherwise be pulled out from under the program still composing into it. A session makes one succession per turn, so an `exec` after a `transitionState` — or a second `exec` — throws `refused`. Bound only when your agent may make agent transitions and has agents it may become, and never while a state machine is driving you. Throws `invalid-argument` for an agent you may not become.

tools.name: fork

parameters.name: prompt
parameters.doc: What the copy is to do instead of what you are doing. It has your whole conversation already, so write the difference rather than a briefing.

tools.doc: Run a copy of yourself, in parallel, on something you will not do yourself. The copy has your model, your tools and a private copy of your whole conversation, so `prompt` is the *difference* rather than a briefing — everything you have worked out is already there. Its handle comes back immediately, but the copy itself starts once this turn's tool results are recorded (the conversation it inherits has to be a complete one), so `waitForSubagents` can only collect it on a later turn — do not wait on it in the program that made it. Throws `limit-exceeded` at the delegation depth cap.

helpers.name: readTextFile

signatures.signature: readTextFile(path: string, options?: { offset?: number; limit?: number; }): string

parameters.name: path
parameters.doc: The file to read. Relative to your workspace, or absolute.

parameters.name: options
parameters.doc: The window of lines to read; omit it to read the whole file.

fields.name: offset
fields.doc: The 1-based line to start at. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

fields.name: limit
fields.doc: How many lines to return from `offset`. Honoured only under a capped read policy.

helpers.doc: Read a text file and return its contents directly — `readFile` without the variant narrowing, for the common case. Takes the same `offset`/`limit` window options. Throws `invalid-argument` when the path names a picture; use `readFile` to inspect those.

types.name: ToolError
types.declaration: class ToolError extends Error { readonly tool: string; readonly code: ToolErrorCode; constructor(tool: string, code: ToolErrorCode, message: string); toJSON(): { name: string; tool: string; code: ToolErrorCode; message: string; }; }
types.doc: A gg tool that failed. Thrown by every tool function. Catch it when a failure is expected and branch on {@link ToolError.code}; let it escape when it is not, and gg reports which tool failed and on which line of the program.

members.name: tool
members.doc: The gg tool that failed (`read_file`, `spawn_subagent`, …).

members.name: code
members.doc: The failure class, so a catch site branches on a value rather than on prose.

types.name: MemoryWrite
types.declaration: interface MemoryWrite { name: string; description: string; body: string; code?: string; onUse?: string; }
types.doc: One memory as a program writes it, with the two optional code halves every write accepts.

members.name: name
members.doc: The memory's slug: letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`. It is what every other memory call takes, and no two memories may share one.

members.name: description
members.doc: A one-line description of what the memory holds. Where the run keeps a memory index this is the memory's line in it, and so all you see of the memory until you read it.

members.name: body
members.doc: The memory's contents.

members.name: code
members.doc: A TypeScript module whose exports are bound at `lib.<name>` for the rest of your session, so a helper you get right once you never write again. Omit it, or pass an empty string, for a memory that is only prose. It costs you no context window and counts against no body limit.

members.name: onUse
members.doc: A script gg runs the first time the memory comes into use; whatever it shows you arrives on your next turn. Omit it, or pass an empty string, for a memory that runs nothing.

types.name: ToolErrorCode
types.declaration: type ToolErrorCode = "invalid-argument" | "not-found" | "conflict" | "refused" | "unavailable" | "limit-exceeded" | "io-error" | "other"
types.doc: Why a tool call failed — the `code` on a thrown `ToolError`, and the value a catch site branches on instead of matching on prose. This is the model-facing spelling of the membrane's `ErrorCode`; `errors.ts` assigns one into the other, so `tsc` rejects a membrane arm this union has not learned about.

members.name: "invalid-argument"
members.doc: The arguments were malformed, ill-typed, or out of range — including a path that is absolute or climbs out of the workspace, and an agent name this run does not declare.

members.name: "not-found"
members.doc: The named file, skill, memory, task, epic, issue, subagent, stored program, or documentation entry does not exist.

members.name: "conflict"
members.doc: Well-formed, but in conflict with the current state: an ambiguous edit, a dependency cycle, a duplicate id, a subagent that already returned.

members.name: "refused"
members.doc: gg refused the call on a rule about your state: a compaction in flight that this call is not the one it asked for, a memory call while your memories are read-only, a second ending or hand-over in a turn that already declared one, or a hook that blocked it. A ceiling you ran into is `limit-exceeded`, not this.

members.name: "unavailable"
members.doc: The call exists but this run's capability set does not offer it. You cannot normally reach this: a withheld function is not bound into your scope at all, so it is the host's backstop for a name a program reached anyway.

members.name: "limit-exceeded"
members.doc: A gg-side ceiling was hit: a shell timeout, a store cap, the delegation depth cap, one of the view caps this program spends, or the run's wall-clock budget.

members.name: "io-error"
members.doc: The underlying I/O or process failed.

members.name: "other"
members.doc: The failure was not classified. Reserved for outcomes raised outside a tool implementation (gg's own bridge and degradation paths); nothing you call produces it.

types.name: ShellOutput
types.declaration: interface ShellOutput { exitCode: number | undefined; output: string; truncated: boolean; }
types.doc: What a command `shell` ran reported when it finished.

members.name: exitCode
members.doc: The process's exit status; `undefined` when a signal killed it. Zero means success.

members.name: output
members.doc: Merged stdout-then-stderr, tail-truncated at 16 KiB — or, when the run offloads shell output, at the configured line/character ceiling, with a note naming the files holding the whole of it. Under the default `adaptive` mode a command that succeeded returns just that note.

members.name: truncated
members.doc: Whether the cap cut `output`, dropping the head and keeping the tail.

types.name: FileRead
types.declaration: type FileRead = { kind: "text"; contents: string; firstLine: number; lastLine: number; totalLines: number; byteTruncated: boolean; } | { kind: "image"; mediaType: string; label: string; bytes: number; shown: boolean; notShownReason: string | undefined; }
types.doc: What `readFile` returned: a text file's window, or a picture's metadata. A picture is a different kind of thing from text, so it is a different case rather than a string that happens to be binary — a program that treats an image as text is caught by the `kind` check instead of silently writing an empty string somewhere. Image *bytes* never enter the program: gg attaches the picture to the turn so the model can look at it directly, which is worth far more than base64 in a variable.

members.name: kind
members.doc: This file is text.

members.name: contents
members.doc: The file's text, or just the requested window under a capped read policy.

members.name: firstLine
members.doc: The 1-based first line returned.

members.name: lastLine
members.doc: The 1-based last line returned.

members.name: totalLines
members.doc: The file's total line count, so you know whether to page again.

members.name: byteTruncated
members.doc: A 256 KiB byte ceiling cut the returned text.

members.name: kind
members.doc: This file is a picture; gg shows it to you rather than handing you its bytes.

members.name: mediaType
members.doc: The IANA media type (`image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/gif`, `image/webp`).

members.name: label
members.doc: The short format label (`PNG`, `JPEG`, `GIF`, `WebP`).

members.name: bytes
members.doc: The file's size in bytes.

members.name: shown
members.doc: Whether the picture is being attached to this turn for you to look at.

members.name: notShownReason
members.doc: Why it is not being shown; `undefined` when `shown` is true.

types.name: DirEntry
types.declaration: interface DirEntry { name: string; kind: "file" | "directory" | "other"; }
types.doc: One entry `listDir` found: a bare name — join it with the directory you listed — and its kind.

members.name: name
members.doc: The entry's bare name, with no directory part. Join it with the directory you listed.

members.name: kind
members.doc: What the entry is. `other` covers everything that is neither, a symlink among them.

types.name: MemoryUsage
types.declaration: interface MemoryUsage { count: number; maxCount: number | undefined; totalChars: number; maxTotalChars: number | undefined; indexChars: number | undefined; maxIndexChars: number | undefined; }
types.doc: How much of the run's durable-memory budget is used, after the call that returned it. Every maximum is optional: each limit can be turned off, and a run's memory strategy applies only some of them, so `undefined` means nothing bounds that axis — check before subtracting.

members.name: count
members.doc: Memories currently held.

members.name: maxCount
members.doc: The most memories this run allows, if it limits the count.

members.name: totalChars
members.doc: Characters of body currently held, across all memories.

members.name: maxTotalChars
members.doc: The most characters of body this run allows in total, if it limits the aggregate.

members.name: indexChars
members.doc: Characters the memory index occupies, under a run that keeps one.

members.name: maxIndexChars
members.doc: The most characters the index may occupy, if it is limited.

types.name: MemoryHit
types.declaration: interface MemoryHit { name: string; description: string; matched: number; occurrences: number; excerpt: string; }
types.doc: One memory `searchMemories` matched, and the numbers it was ranked by.

members.name: name
members.doc: The memory's slug — what `readMemory` takes.

members.name: description
members.doc: Its description, or `""` when it was created without one.

members.name: matched
members.doc: How many of your distinct keywords it matched — the primary ranking.

members.name: occurrences
members.doc: How many times those keywords occur in it — the tiebreak.

members.name: excerpt
members.doc: A short window of the memory around its first match.

types.name: TaskStatus
types.declaration: type TaskStatus = "pending" | "in_progress" | "done"
types.doc: Where a task stands.

members.name: "pending"
members.doc: Not started. Every task begins here.

members.name: "in_progress"
members.doc: Being worked on now.

members.name: "done"
members.doc: Finished. Tasks blocked on it become actionable once all their blockers are done.

types.name: TaskUsage
types.declaration: interface TaskUsage { count: number; maxTasks: number; }
types.doc: How much of the run's task budget is used, after the call that returned it.

members.name: count
members.doc: Tasks currently on the list.

members.name: maxTasks
members.doc: The most tasks this run allows.

types.name: IssueStatus
types.declaration: type IssueStatus = "open" | "in_progress" | "done"
types.doc: Where an issue stands.

members.name: "open"
members.doc: Not started, and dispatchable once its blockers are done.

members.name: "in_progress"
members.doc: Dispatched, with its assigned agent working on it.

members.name: "done"
members.doc: Finished and, where this run requires reviewers, approved.

types.name: BoardUsage
types.declaration: interface BoardUsage { epics: number; maxEpics: number; issues: number; maxIssues: number; }
types.doc: How much of the run's board budget is used, after the call that returned it.

members.name: epics
members.doc: Epics currently on the board.

members.name: maxEpics
members.doc: The most epics this run allows.

members.name: issues
members.doc: Issues currently on the board.

members.name: maxIssues
members.doc: The most issues this run allows.

types.name: EpicCreated
types.declaration: interface EpicCreated { id: string; board: BoardUsage; }
types.doc: An epic that was just created: the id its prefix resolved to, and the board budget.

members.name: id
members.doc: The epic's id — the prefix you gave, upper-cased (`auth` → `AUTH`). Group issues under it with this, and its issues are numbered from it (`AUTH-1`).

members.name: board
members.doc: How much of the board budget is used.

types.name: IssueCreated
types.declaration: interface IssueCreated { id: string; board: BoardUsage; }
types.doc: An issue that was just created: the id the board assigned it, and the board budget.

members.name: id
members.doc: The id the board assigned (`AUTH-1`) — you do not choose it. Use it to block later issues on this one, or to wait for it.

members.name: board
members.doc: How much of the board budget is used.

types.name: ReclaimReport
types.declaration: interface ReclaimReport { items: number; reclaimedTokens: number; paths: string[]; detail: string; }
types.doc: What a context reclaim actually freed from the live context window.

members.name: items
members.doc: Context items dropped from the live window.

members.name: reclaimedTokens
members.doc: Approximately how many tokens that freed.

members.name: paths
members.doc: The workspace paths whose views were evicted. Empty for an archive.

members.name: detail
members.doc: The prose summary of what was reclaimed.

types.name: TurnRange
types.declaration: interface TurnRange { from: number; to: number; }
types.doc: An inclusive span of turn numbers, the unit `archiveThread` moves out of the window. The numbers are the ones on the header of every result you are given, so `{ from: 4, to: 19 }` means exactly the turns you can see numbered 4 through 19 — both ends included.

members.name: from
members.doc: The first turn in the span.

members.name: to
members.doc: The last turn in the span, inclusive.

types.name: ArchiveHit
types.declaration: interface ArchiveHit { seq: number; role: "system" | "user" | "assistant" | "tool"; text: string; }
types.doc: One archived message that matched a search.

members.name: seq
members.doc: The archived message's sequence number.

members.name: role
members.doc: Who said it.

members.name: text
members.doc: The message text.

types.name: ArchiveSearch
types.declaration: interface ArchiveSearch { archiveEmpty: boolean; hits: ArchiveHit[]; }
types.doc: What `searchArchive` found.

members.name: archiveEmpty
members.doc: Nothing has been archived yet, so there was nothing to search. Deliberately distinct from a search that ran and matched nothing, so you do not archive again believing the first archive failed.

members.name: hits
members.doc: The matches, most recent first, at most 8.

types.name: ViewKind
types.declaration: type ViewKind = "file" | "text" | "docs"
types.doc: Which of the three kinds a view is. The taxonomy is closed at three on purpose: everything on disk is a file, everything a program can compute is a string, and documentation is neither — gg holds it. A directory listing, a command's output, a child agent's answer, a table you assembled are all **text** views; what `view.openDocsView` opens is a **docs** view.

members.name: "file"
members.doc: A file you opened; its selector is the path.

members.name: "text"
members.doc: A value you showed yourself; its selector is the label you gave it.

members.name: "docs"
members.doc: A function's documentation; its selector is the function's name.

types.name: ViewRegion
types.declaration: interface ViewRegion { offset: number; limit: number; }
types.doc: The window of lines a **paged** file view covers; absent for a whole-file view.

members.name: offset
members.doc: The 1-based first line the view shows.

members.name: limit
members.doc: How many lines it shows.

types.name: OpenView
types.declaration: interface OpenView { kind: ViewKind; selector: string; tokens: number; region?: ViewRegion; }
types.doc: One view open in your context window, as `view.current()` reports it.

members.name: kind
members.doc: Whether it is a file, text, or documentation view.

members.name: selector
members.doc: What `view.close` takes: a file's path, a text view's label, or a docs view's function name.

members.name: tokens
members.doc: Roughly what holding it costs you, in tokens.

members.name: region
members.doc: The line window a paged file view covers; absent for a whole-file view and for text views.

types.name: SubagentHandle
types.declaration: interface SubagentHandle { id: string; slot: string; modelId: string; }
types.doc: A child agent that was spawned and is now running in parallel.

members.name: id
members.doc: The child's id — pass it to `waitForSubagents` or `sendMessage`.

members.name: slot
members.doc: The agent profile it runs as.

members.name: modelId
members.doc: The model actually bound to that agent.

types.name: AgentEnding
types.declaration: type AgentEnding = "completed" | "exhausted" | "timed_out" | "model_error" | "auth_error" | "limit_exceeded"
types.doc: How a child agent's loop ended — gg's own six words, as the native path also reports them.

members.name: "completed"
members.doc: It finished normally: it called `finish`, and its summary is what it returned.

members.name: "exhausted"
members.doc: It hit the per-run turn ceiling.

members.name: "timed_out"
members.doc: It passed its wall-clock deadline.

members.name: "model_error"
members.doc: A model turn failed.

members.name: "auth_error"
members.doc: The run's credential was refused.

members.name: "limit_exceeded"
members.doc: An execution ceiling stopped it — consecutive errors, error rate, or cost.

types.name: SubagentResult
types.declaration: interface SubagentResult { id: string; status: AgentEnding | undefined; summary: string; }
types.doc: One child agent's collected result.

members.name: id
members.doc: The child's id.

members.name: status
members.doc: How it finished; `undefined` when it produced no return value at all.

members.name: summary
members.doc: Its final message.

types.name: ProgramSummary
types.declaration: interface ProgramSummary { turn: number; lines: number; chars: number; ok: boolean; error?: string; }
types.doc: One program you have already run, as `programs.history()` lists it. It describes the program's **shape**, never its source: a directory that inlined every program would put the whole session back in front of you, which is the one thing the library exists to avoid. Fetch the source you actually want with `programs.get(turn)`.

members.name: turn
members.doc: The turn it ran on — what `programs.get` takes.

members.name: lines
members.doc: How many lines of source it was.

members.name: chars
members.doc: How many characters of source it was.

members.name: ok
members.doc: Whether it ran to its end, with no uncaught throw and no sandbox ceiling stopping it.

members.name: error
members.doc: The error it ended with, when it did not run to its end.

types.name: FunctionSummary
types.declaration: interface FunctionSummary { name: string; summary: string; }
types.doc: One function in an API object's directory, as `list()` returns it. It is the entry of the one function every API object carries whatever a run enables, so a program can always discover what it has. The summary is one line; the whole documentation of a function — every shape it may be called in, what to put in each argument, and the types it refers to — is a view, opened with `openDocsView`.

members.name: name
members.doc: The function name on its object — `readFile` in `fs.readFile(...)`.

members.name: summary
members.doc: One line saying what it does: the first sentence of its documentation.
